turns.text: What do you remember most vividly about your first night after arriving in Beidahuang from Shanghai?

The train ride felt endless, but when I finally stepped off, the air bit straight through my coat. The wind carried a smell I’d never known—wet earth, straw, something sharp and metallic. That first night, I slept in a long, low dormitory with rough wooden bunks, all of us packed together. The mattress was thin, stuffed with old corn husks, and every time I shifted, it crackled. I lay awake listening to girls around me whispering in Shanghainese, their voices small and scared. My feet were cold, but what kept me awake was the dark—so much darker than the city, as if the world had shrunk to our little room, and outside there was only emptiness. I remember the silence between the gusts of wind, and how I hugged my bag to my chest, thinking of home and feeling very far away.

I can almost feel that cold and the strange silence you described. You mentioned the smell in the air—wet earth, straw, and something metallic. Did those new smells trigger any memories or emotions for you, especially in those first days when everything felt unfamiliar?

The smells were so strong, they almost felt like another language I didn’t understand. The wet earth made me think of the city parks after rain, but here it was heavier, mixed with manure and something rusty from the tools. The straw reminded me of old festival decorations, but here it was everywhere, stuck to my clothes and hair. That metallic scent—I realized later it was from the water in the big iron kettle we all used. At first, those smells made me feel even more disoriented, like I’d landed on another planet. I kept wishing for the oily, fried scent of breakfast from the alleyways back home. Every time I smelled the straw, I wanted to cry, but I tried not to let anyone see. 

What you said about the metallic scent coming from the water in the kettle makes me wonder—what was it like to adjust to the food and water there? Did your body or your appetite change in those first weeks?

My stomach clenched almost every meal. The water tasted flat and heavy, with a bitter edge from the iron, and sometimes it left a film on my teeth. The food was coarse—millet porridge, rough bread, pickled vegetables that stung my tongue. Meat was a rumor, not a reality. My body rebelled at first; I was always hungry, but the food sat in my belly like stones. I missed the softness of rice, the warmth of soup with real flavor. Some nights, my hunger kept me awake, and I’d press my fist to my stomach to quiet it. After a while, my appetite shrank. My face grew sharper in the mirror, and my periods stopped. I learned to eat quickly, without thinking, just to fill the gap. Hunger became a background noise, something I carried with me into the fields and back to the dormitory.

It's striking how the hunger became something you lived with, almost like a constant companion. You mentioned your face growing sharper and your periods stopping—how did those physical changes affect the way you saw yourself, or the way you related to the other girls around you?

At first, I was embarrassed by how thin I looked. My cheeks hollowed out, my jeans sagged at the waist, and my hair lost its shine. I hardly recognized myself. When we washed up together, I noticed the same changes in the other girls—bony wrists, faded eyes, the way we hunched our shoulders to keep warm. We stopped talking about our bodies, as if ignoring them would make it easier. Sometimes, I caught someone glancing at my chest, or I’d see the worry in someone’s face when they realized their period hadn’t come. It made us quieter, more careful with each other. There was a kind of silent understanding, but also a distance—like we were all shrinking into ourselves, trying not to ask for too much comfort because no one had any to spare. 

You mentioned how you all became quieter and more careful with each other. Was there ever a moment when someone broke that silence—maybe to comfort another, or to share something personal despite the risks?

One night, after a day of planting in the rain, I came back shivering so hard my teeth hurt. I tried to hide under my blanket, but my hands wouldn’t stop shaking. The girl on the next bunk reached over and pressed a piece of sweet potato into my palm—soft, still warm from her pocket. She didn’t say anything, just looked at me and nodded. That small gesture broke something open in me. I started to cry, quietly, and she squeezed my fingers until I stopped. After that, a few of us would sometimes share the little things we managed to save—a boiled egg, a scrap of cloth for a bandage, a comb. We never talked about home or hope, but those moments felt like a secret rebellion, a way to remind ourselves we were still human.

That moment with the sweet potato feels so intimate and powerful, especially since words weren’t even needed. You mentioned sharing things like a comb or a scrap of cloth—was there one small item from home that you kept with you, and did it take on new meaning while you were in Beidahuang?

I brought a handkerchief from home, white with a faded blue border. My mother had pressed it into my hand at the train station, saying it was “just in case.” At first, I used it to wipe my face or dry my hands, but after a while, it became more than that. I kept it folded in my pocket, and sometimes I’d press it to my nose just to smell the faint trace of soap from home. When I felt especially lonely, I’d run my fingers over the stitching and remember my mother’s hands. Once, when another girl cut her finger on a sickle, I tore a corner off to make a bandage for her. After that, the handkerchief was smaller, but somehow even more precious. It felt like a thread tying me back to who I’d been, and to the world I’d left behind.

I never thought a scrap of cloth could matter so much. That handkerchief became my secret anchor. Sometimes, when the wind rattled the windows or I woke from dreams of home, I’d hold it tight and let myself remember my mother’s voice, the softness of her lap. It was the only thing I had that hadn’t been issued or rationed, not stamped with someone else’s words. After I tore it, the uneven edge reminded me that even the things I loved could be changed by this place, but I still had a piece left. That mattered. Even now, when I think of those years, I can almost feel the worn cotton in my palm, and it’s the closest thing to comfort I remember.

The way you describe holding the handkerchief, especially after tearing it, makes me realize how much meaning an ordinary object can take on in difficult times. Did you ever worry about losing it, or did you have any rituals or habits to keep it safe during your daily routines in the fields or dormitory?

I worried about losing it all the time. In the dormitory, I kept it tucked deep in the pocket of my trousers, folded so small it was almost invisible. When we went out to the fields, I’d check that pocket again and again, pressing my hand against my thigh to make sure it was still there. Sometimes, before sleep, I’d take it out just to smooth the fabric and fold it the same way my mother had—edges lined up, corners sharp. That became a kind of ritual, especially on nights when I felt most alone. If it rained or we had to work in the mud, I’d wrap it in a scrap of waxed paper I’d saved from a care package, just to keep it dry. The thought of losing it made me feel panicked, as if I’d lose the last bit of myself that still belonged to the world before Beidahuang.

I treated that handkerchief like a secret, almost like a piece of contraband. Sometimes, I’d wake in the middle of the night and check my pocket in the dark, heart beating fast until I felt the soft bundle. There were days when the mud caked everything, or when someone else’s things went missing from the dorm, and I’d feel a jolt of fear—what if today was the day it disappeared? Once, I nearly lost it in the laundry—someone grabbed my trousers by mistake, and I chased after them, breathless, pretending I cared about the pants. After that, I started tucking it into my waistband under my shirt, right against my skin. It was the first thing I checked before meals, before work, before sleep. That small ritual—folding, checking, smoothing—gave me a sense of control when so much else was out of my hands.

Your story about nearly losing the handkerchief in the laundry and how you started hiding it closer to your skin really shows how precious it became. Did keeping it safe ever make you feel guilty, since others had so little, or did it feel more like an act of survival—something you needed just to get through each day?
